key_facts: Drugs cause about 10–20% of acquired hyperpigmentation; colours and sites are clues.
**Minocycline**: blue-grey on scars, shins and sclera; **amiodarone**: slate-grey on sun-exposed face; **hydroxychloroquine**: grey-blue shins and palate.
Chemotherapy (bleomycin flagellate streaks, 5-FU), zidovudine (nails), clofazimine (red-brown), heavy metals (argyria).
Fixed drug eruption leaves round grey-brown patches at the same sites.
Stop or switch the drug with the prescriber; pigmentation fades slowly (months–years) or may be permanent; photoprotection.

ul: **Amiodarone** causes two linked skin problems: **Phototoxicity** — burning/erythema within hours of sun exposure (UVA); up to 30–75% of patients; **Blue-grey (slate) pigmentation** of sun-exposed skin (~1–10%), usually after **months of treatment and high cumulative doses** (>40–160 g)
The case: a 50-year-old man in a sunny country, 3 months after starting amiodarone (dose recently increased), with increased sun sensitivity and a facial photo showing blue-grey discoloration.
**"It'll go as soon as the drug stops"**: dermal pigment can persist for years.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Drugs pigment skin by **increasing melanin, depositing themselves, or forming drug–iron–melanin complexes**.

mech.t: Some drugs stimulate melanocytes (oral contraceptives in melasma, chemotherapy).
Drug or metabolites deposit in the dermis (amiodarone lipofuscin, gold, silver).
Drug, iron and melanin bind together in dermal macrophages (minocycline).
Inflammatory reactions leave melanin in the dermis (fixed drug eruption).

ul: Amiodarone and its metabolite **desethylamiodarone** absorb **UVA (300–400 nm)** and generate reactive oxygen species → phototoxic injury.

Both are **lipophilic**, with an extremely **long half-life (~50 days, range 20–100)**. They accumulate in dermal macrophages as **lipofuscin-like granules with drug–lipid complexes**, and melanin rises → blue-grey colour.

sections.title: Clinical features
blocks: Burning, erythema and prickling minutes to hours after sun, even through glass (UVA). Later, **blue-grey/violaceous** colour of the **face (nose, cheeks), ears and backs of hands**. Also look for other amiodarone toxicity: thyroid (hypo-/hyperthyroidism), liver, lung (pneumonitis/fibrosis), eyes (corneal microdeposits, optic neuropathy), peripheral neuropathy.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Clinical (history + distribution). Biopsy only if doubtful (yellow-brown granules in macrophages; Fontana-Masson). Check **TFT, LFT**, CXR ± PFT, and arrange ophthalmology review per the amiodarone monitoring schedule (BNF: TFT/LFT every 6 months).

sections.title: Differential diagnoses

ul: **Exogenous:** systemic drugs — phototoxic or photoallergic (see *Drug-induced photosensitivity — thiazide case*); topical agents — fragrances, sunscreens (photoallergic), **phytophotodermatitis** (psoralens in limes, figs, celery, giant hogweed), tar
**Idiopathic photodermatoses:** **polymorphic light eruption (PLE)**, actinic prurigo, **chronic actinic dermatitis**, solar urticaria, hydroa vacciniforme.
**Genetic:** xeroderma pigmentosum, albinism, Bloom, Cockayne and Rothmund–Thomson syndromes.

blocks: **Blue-grey pigmentation DDx:** **minocycline**, antimalarials (hydroxychloroquine — shins/palate), phenothiazines (chlorpromazine), tricyclics (imipramine), argyria (silver), chrysiasis (gold), ochronosis (hydroquinone), Addison's (brown, not blue — the [skin signs of systemic disease](condition:dermatomyositis) notes), haemochromatosis, cyanosis, methaemoglobinaemia (dapsone).

sections.title: Management

ol: **Do not stop amiodarone yourself.** Discuss with the **cardiologist** (dose reduction or an alternative antiarrhythmic, rate/rhythm strategy, ablation).
The BNF advises avoiding sun exposure **during treatment and for several months after stopping** (long half-life).

**Pigmentation** fades very slowly over months to years after stopping or reducing the dose, and may be permanent. Camouflage makeup; Q-switched/picosecond laser (specialist, private) for persistent cases.
**Monitoring:** TFT, LFT (6-monthly), annual eye check, CXR baseline. Yellow Card.

blocks: Counselling, photoprotection, monitoring, liaison with cardiology, Yellow Card. Antiarrhythmic changes are specialist/shared-care decisions.

refer.t: New pigmentation on amiodarone: check **thyroid and liver function** and ask about breathlessness (amiodarone toxicity).
Generalised pigmentation with tiredness, weight loss or low blood pressure: exclude **Addison’s disease**.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: New pigmentation on amiodarone: check **thyroid and liver function** and ask about breathlessness (amiodarone toxicity).
Generalised pigmentation with tiredness, weight loss or low blood pressure: exclude **Addison’s disease**.

blocks: Blistering phototoxicity; new breathlessness/cough (pneumonitis); visual change (optic neuropathy); thyroid symptoms; jaundice.

ul: Cosmetic distress; marker of cumulative dose (amiodarone).

pearls: "Amiodarone sensitivity **goes through window glass**" — UVA, so driving and office windows count.
Effects persist for months after stopping (half-life ~50 days), and the pigment for longer.
Counsel at the first supply — the BNF lists phototoxicity among the amiodarone counselling points.

quiz.q: When should you think of Drug-induced pigmentation (amiodarone, minocycline)?
quiz.a: Blue-grey or slate discolouration of the face or sun-exposed skin in someone on long-term amiodarone or minocycline.
Drug or drug–melanin complexes deposited in the dermis, often worsened by UV light.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Medication review with the prescriber (amiodarone is often essential); sun protection; explain fading takes months to years.
Other amiodarone toxicity (thyroid, liver, lung, eyes); Addison’s disease or haemochromatosis as non-drug causes.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: New pigmentation on amiodarone: check **thyroid and liver function** and ask about breathlessness (amiodarone toxicity).
